title: Onboarding checklist in Console (draft) — Hosted API activation
content:
Context / why this doc exists
- We’re running the Lifecycle Growth Experiments sprint (4 weeks) and need a consistent in-console onboarding “next best action” surface that:
  (1) drives first successful request + 100k tokens within 7 days,
  (2) reduces time-to-first-token (TTFT),
  (3) can be A/B tested + feature-flagged cleanly.
- This doc proposes an “Onboarding Checklist” component that can either:
  - live as a persistent checklist widget (preferred), OR
  - be rendered as a series of nudges (fallback if checklist is too heavy for sprint timeline).

Non-goals / guardrails
- Not a full onboarding re-architecture.
- Not a docs overhaul.
- Not adding new billing/pricing steps.
- Must respect email preferences / unsub and privacy constraints (no creepy messaging, no “we saw you do X on your laptop”).
- Avoid spamming existing activated accounts and avoid conflicts with enterprise onboarding flows.

Primary user segment
- New self-serve developers using Hosted API who sign up via web and land in Console.
- Exclusions (see eligibility rules): existing high-volume accounts, sales-assisted enterprise opportunities, Private/Dedicated deployments.

Checklist goals + success criteria (product)
- Primary: lift % of new signups completing:
  - First successful request within 7 days
  - First 100k tokens within 7 days
- Secondary:
  - Reduce time from signup → first request (and TTFT once request is made)
  - Improve D7/D30 return usage
  - Increase “healthy setup” actions: enabling streaming, viewing usage dashboard (and reducing confusion/support tickets)

Proposed UX surface
- Placement options (ordered by preference):
  1) Right rail widget on “Overview” / landing page after login
  2) Top section of API Keys page (but we risk blocking the primary action)
  3) Inline module on “Get started” page (if that page exists for all users)
- Behavior:
  - Always visible until completed or dismissed
  - Shows 3–5 steps max (keep it short)
  - Each step has a single CTA leading to a console page or docs link
  - Completion state should be deterministic and event-driven (no manual checkboxes)
  - Dismiss should be available, but we should confirm what “dismiss” means (hide forever vs snooze)

Recommended checklist steps (v1)
Principle: each item must map to an observable state change + clean event instrumentation.

Step 1 — Create an API key
- Rationale: highest friction early gate; must be unblocked and highly visible.
- Completion condition: API key created (project scope).
- CTA target: Console → API Keys → Create key.
- Copy options:
  A) “Create an API key”
     Supporting: “You’ll use this key to call the Redwood API from your app.”
     CTA: “Create key”
  B) “Get your API key”
     Supporting: “Takes ~10 seconds.”
     CTA: “Generate key”
  C) “Create API key to start sending requests”
     Supporting: “Keys can be rotated anytime.”
     CTA: “Create API key”
- Notes:
  - Do not show full key in checklist UI; link to keys screen.
  - If they already have a key, skip this step entirely.

Step 2 — Make your first request (Hello World)
- Rationale: direct activation lever; aligns with email CTA + quickstart snippet.
- Completion condition: first successful request event observed (chat/completions/embeddings counts) OR “first_token_generated” depending on final event taxonomy.
- CTA target: “Quickstart” modal or code snippet (language toggle) OR docs link + copy button.
- Copy options:
  A) “Send your first request”
     Supporting: “Copy a minimal curl example and stream a response.”
     CTA: “View example”
  B) “Run a Hello World request”
     Supporting: “See output in seconds.”
     CTA: “Get snippet”
  C) “Test the API from your terminal”
     Supporting: “We’ll guide you step-by-step.”
     CTA: “Open quickstart”
- Implementation note (important): if we can embed a “Try it” request runner in-console, great, but for sprint timeline we can start with:
  - code snippet + docs link + “Copy” button + a lightweight confirmation “Copied” state.
  - still need a real completion event based on successful request server-side (not “clicked”).

Step 3 — Enable streaming (optional but recommended)
- Rationale: improves perceived latency and dev experience; aligns with “developer-first” positioning.
- Completion condition: user toggles “streaming enabled” in example code OR uses streaming parameter in first request event.
- CTA target: docs section “Streaming responses” or quickstart snippet toggle.
- Copy options:
  A) “Enable streaming responses”
     Supporting: “Lower perceived latency for chat-style apps.”
     CTA: “Show me how”
  B) “Stream tokens as they generate”
     Supporting: “Better UX and faster time-to-first-token.”
     CTA: “Enable streaming”
- Note: if we can’t reliably detect streaming usage in events yet, treat this as a “nudge” not a checklist step (or mark complete on click, but that’s weaker and may mislead).

Step 4 — Check usage + cost (introduce observability early)
- Rationale: reduces surprise bills and builds trust; also creates a return reason (dashboard).
- Completion condition: user visits Usage dashboard page (unique visit within onboarding window).
- CTA target: Console → Usage dashboard.
- Copy options:
  A) “View usage and tokens”
     Supporting: “Track latency, tokens, and spend as you test.”
     CTA: “Open usage”
  B) “See your usage breakdown”
     Supporting: “Understand cost per request.”
     CTA: “View dashboard”

Step 5 — (Optional) Set a usage alert / limit
- Rationale: “safe sandboxing” for new users; lowers anxiety.
- Completion condition: user sets a limit/alert.
- CTA: Console → Billing/limits.
- Copy options:
  A) “Set a usage limit (optional)”
     Supporting: “Avoid surprises while you explore.”
     CTA: “Set limit”
  B) “Add a usage alert”
     Supporting: “Get notified as you approach a threshold.”
     CTA: “Create alert”
- Note: only include if the UI is already present and not confusing; otherwise this becomes scope creep.

Step ordering rules (dynamic)
- Show max 4 steps at a time.
- Prioritize:
  1) Create API key (if missing)
  2) First request (always until complete)
  3) Usage dashboard
  4) Streaming (if we can measure)
  5) Usage limit (optional)
- If “Create API key” is complete at first render, start with “Send your first request.”

Eligibility rules (who sees checklist)
- Must be logged in to Console.
- Must be a Hosted API org/project (exclude Dedicated/Private consoles if we have separate surfaces).
- Primary cohort:
  - Signup age: 0–14 days (proposed default). Open question: should we cap at 7 days for focus?
  - Has NOT completed “first successful request” OR has completed it but not “first 100k tokens” (see phases below).
- Exclusions / suppressions:
  - Accounts flagged as sales-assisted enterprise opportunity (per Jordan/Stephanie rules); do not show growthy onboarding if a CSM/AE is driving onboarding.
  - Internal employees / test orgs.
  - High-volume orgs (e.g., already >1M tokens) — they don’t need it.
  - Users who dismissed checklist (but define dismissal behavior).

Phases (proposed)
Phase 0: Pre-activation
- Definition: no successful request yet.
- Checklist emphasizes API key + first request.

Phase 1: Post-first-request (activation acceleration)
- Definition: at least 1 successful request, but <100k tokens and/or no return visit.
- Checklist shifts to:
  - “Hit 100k tokens” (or “Run your first real integration”) + “View usage” + “Enable streaming.”
- Copy must be careful: avoid sounding like we’re pushing consumption for its own sake. Frame as “validate integration” and “measure performance.”

Phase 2: Graduated
- Definition: first 100k tokens completed OR account is clearly active.
- Checklist disappears (or is replaced with a lighter “Tips” module).

UX details / states
- Progress indicator: “2 of 4 complete” with checkmarks.
- Item states:
  - Default
  - Completed (check icon)
  - Loading (when we’re waiting for server event confirmation)
  - Error (rare; likely avoid showing errors in checklist—just keep incomplete)
- Dismissal:
  - Option A: “Dismiss” hides for 30 days (snooze)
  - Option B: “Dismiss” hides forever for that user+org
  - Option C: “Not helpful” opens mini feedback (free text) — might be too much for sprint
- Recommendation: snooze 30 days; re-show only if still unactivated after 7 days? Need to decide.

Copy guidelines (from messaging principles)
- Keep it developer-first, practical, and outcome-oriented.
- Approved themes:
  - Fast path to first working output
  - Performance + reliability trust signals (“streaming”, “usage breakdown”)
  - Predictable cost controls
- Avoid:
  - Overpromising “best latency” without specifics
  - Any language implying we observe private code/repo contents

Event instrumentation (minimum needed)
- For each step we need:
  - Impression: checklist_rendered
  - Interaction: checklist_step_clicked (step_id, placement)
  - Completion: derived from actual product events (api_key_created, first_request_success, usage_page_viewed, streaming_used, usage_limit_set)
- Required properties (draft):
  - org_id, user_id, project_id
  - cohort_id / experiment_flag
  - signup_date_bucket
  - region
  - surface_location (overview_right_rail, etc.)
- NOTE: This doc doesn’t finalize event names; follow ENG-10492 draft taxonomy.

Experiment / rollout plan (high level)
- Phase 1 (sprint): behind feature flag, with holdout.
  - 50% eligible users see checklist (treatment), 50% holdout.
  - Alternatively: ramp 10% → 25% → 50% after 24h metric sanity checks.
- Success metrics:
  - Activation lift vs holdout
  - Time-to-first-request median
  - Downstream: first 100k tokens within 7 days
  - Secondary: usage page visits, streaming adoption
- Guardrails:
  - Support ticket volume (esp. API key creation issues)
  - Any increase in console errors on key pages
  - If checklist blocks key creation or overlays incorrectly, roll back immediately (see prior UX edge case risk).

Open questions / decisions needed
1) Do we implement as a true checklist component or keep it as sequential nudges?
   - Checklist is better long-term; nudges are easier to ship fast.
2) What is the canonical definition of “first successful request”?
   - Must be consistent with the activation funnel dashboard.
3) Can we reliably detect “streaming enabled” usage in eventing?
   - If not, treat streaming as a click-through info nudge.
4) Dismiss semantics:
   - snooze vs forever; and should it be per-user or per-org?
5) Where should this live in Console nav?
   - Overview right rail is ideal; need to confirm that page exists for all orgs and isn’t already overloaded.
6) What happens for orgs with multiple users?
   - If one user completes first request, do we mark checklist complete for other users in same org? (Probably yes for org-level milestones; user-level for UI onboarding.)

Notes from early feedback (unstructured)
- “Make the first request snippet impossible to mess up” (include model name, endpoint, and auth header; show the exact place API key goes).
- “Don’t ask me to do 7 steps; I’ll ignore it.”
- “Seeing usage/cost early builds trust.”

Next actions (as of last edit)
- Kenji + Marissa: confirm UI layout + copy length constraints for right rail.
- Dylan/Ethan: confirm feasibility + timing for checklist component vs reuse nudge component.
- Nadia/Logan: lock step completion conditions and event property requirements.
- Ben: align this with email CTAs so the experience feels consistent (same language: ‘first request’ / ‘hello world’).
